## Remarks

The diagram displays the Cartesian square together with the test maps in the definition. For any scheme $T$ and morphisms $a:T\to X$ and $b:T\to Y$ satisfying $fa=gb$, the dashed morphism $h:T\to P$ is uniquely determined by $ph=a$ and $qh=b$; the square commutes because $fp=gq$. All arrows are morphisms of schemes. This illustrates the defining property and does not assert existence of a fibre product.

```tikzcd
T \arrow[dr, dashed, "{\exists!\,h}"] \arrow[drr, bend left=20, "a"] \arrow[ddr, bend right=20, "b"'] & & \\
& P=X\times_S Y \arrow[r, "p"] \arrow[d, "q"'] & X \arrow[d, "f"] \\
& Y \arrow[r, "g"'] & S
```

## Remarks

The Cartesian square in the statement is illustrated below; the maps are $\Gamma_u=(\operatorname{id}_X,u)$ and $H=(u\operatorname{pr}_X,\operatorname{pr}_Y)$.

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[scale=1.8, transform shape, column sep=large, row sep=large]
X \arrow[r, "\Gamma_u"] \arrow[d, "u"'] & X\times_S Y \arrow[d, "H"] \\
Y \arrow[r, "\Delta_{Y/S}"'] & Y\times_S Y
\end{tikzcd}
```

Both composites are $(u,u):X\to Y\times_S Y$. The square is Cartesian by the test-map argument in the proof, which is independent of this illustration.
